title: Transport Layer: TCP vs UDP
summary: TCP guarantees delivery; UDP just sends fast. Learn what the transport layer does, how ports and sockets work, and when to pick each protocol.

blocks.markdown:
The **transport layer** is Layer 4 in the [osi-tcpip-models](osi-tcpip-models) stack. It moves data **process-to-process** — not just machine-to-machine.

- IP gets a packet to the right **machine**; the transport layer gets it to the right **app**.
- Two protocols: **TCP** (reliable, ordered) and **UDP** (fast, no guarantees).
- Choosing wrong costs you: TCP overhead hurts real-time apps; UDP data loss hurts banking.

IP knows how to reach a **host** (machine). But your laptop runs a browser, a game, and a music player at once — IP alone can't tell them apart.

The transport layer uses a **port number** (0–65535) to direct each packet to the correct process. Every running network app claims a port.

- Sender attaches: source port + destination port.
- The OS delivers to whichever process owns that destination port.

blocks.subTitle: What is a port?
blocks.markdown:
A **port** is a 16-bit number (0–65535) that identifies a specific process on a host.

- **Well-known ports** (0–1023): reserved for system services. HTTP=80, HTTPS=443, DNS=53, SSH=22.
- **Registered ports** (1024–49151): app-specific conventions.
- **Ephemeral ports** (49152–65535): temporary ports the OS assigns to clients for each outgoing connection.

blocks.subTitle: What is a socket?
blocks.markdown:
A **socket** is the combination of an **IP address + port number**. It uniquely identifies one endpoint of a connection.

- A connection is a pair of sockets: `(client IP:port) ↔ (server IP:port)`.
- The OS represents a socket as a file descriptor your app can read/write.
- The same server port (e.g. 443) can serve thousands of connections because each client brings a different IP or ephemeral port.

See [sockets-network-programming](sockets-network-programming) for deeper usage.

**Multiplexing**: the sender bundles data from many app processes into one stream of packets — each stamped with source and destination ports.

**Demultiplexing**: the receiver reads the destination port and routes each incoming packet to the right process.

Think of it as a post office: many letters come in (mux), the postman reads the apartment number (demux) and slides each under the right door.

**TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)** provides reliable, ordered, connection-oriented delivery.

- **Connection-oriented**: a 3-way handshake (SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK) must complete before data flows.
- **Reliable**: every segment gets an **acknowledgement (ACK)**; missing ones are retransmitted.
- **Ordered**: sequence numbers ensure the receiver reassembles bytes in the correct order.
- **Flow & congestion control**: TCP slows down when the network or receiver is overwhelmed.

blocks.subTitle: The 3-way handshake
blocks.markdown:
TCP opens every connection with a 3-way handshake before sending any data.

<<< Image: simple vertical sequence diagram, two columns labelled Client and Server, blue/grey palette. Three arrows: 1 SYN (left to right), 2 SYN-ACK (right to left), 3 ACK (left to right). Label below: 'Connection established — data can now flow'. Clean whitespace, minimal labels. >>>

- **SYN**: client picks a random sequence number and asks to connect.
- **SYN-ACK**: server acknowledges and picks its own sequence number.
- **ACK**: client confirms. Both sides are synchronized.

**UDP (User Datagram Protocol)** is connectionless and best-effort — it sends and forgets.

- **No handshake**: data goes out immediately.
- **No ACKs or retransmits**: lost packets are gone.
- **No ordering**: packets can arrive out of sequence.
- **Very low overhead**: the UDP header is 8 bytes vs TCP's 20+ bytes.

If reliability matters, the application layer must add it on top.

The central trade-off: reliability vs speed.

| Feature | TCP | UDP |
|---|---|---|
| Connection | 3-way handshake | None |
| Reliability | ACKs + retransmit | Best-effort |
| Ordering | Guaranteed | Not guaranteed |
| Speed | Slower (overhead) | Faster (lean) |
| Use case | HTTP, SSH, email | DNS, video, games |

blocks.subTitle: When to use each
blocks.markdown:
Pick **TCP** when losing data is unacceptable: web pages, file transfers, database queries, SSH sessions, email.

Pick **UDP** when speed or low latency beats correctness:
- **DNS lookups** — one small request, retry is cheap if it fails.
- **Live video / audio streaming** — a late frame is worse than a dropped one.
- **Online games** — stale position data is useless; send fresh instead.
- **IoT sensor bursts** — high-volume, loss-tolerant readings.

Memorize these well-known ports — they appear in interviews and config files constantly.

| Port | Protocol | Use |
|---|---|---|
| 80 | HTTP / TCP | Web (unencrypted) |
| 443 | HTTPS / TCP | Web (TLS encrypted) |
| 53 | DNS / UDP | Domain name lookups |
| 22 | SSH / TCP | Secure shell access |

Common mistakes:

- **"UDP is unreliable, so never use it."** Wrong — video calls and games deliberately accept packet loss for lower latency.
- **"A server can only handle one connection per port."** Wrong — the socket is a 4-tuple (src IP, src port, dst IP, dst port); thousands of clients can share port 443.
- **"TCP is always slower in practice."** For a single request-response (like DNS), UDP wins; for bulk data, TCP's flow control can actually saturate bandwidth more efficiently.

blocks.subTitle: TCP vs UDP — when to use each
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: TCP vs UDP — when would you choose each?**

**TCP** when data must arrive complete and in order: HTTP, file downloads, SSH. **UDP** when low latency beats completeness: live video, DNS, multiplayer games.

Best answer: ask "is a lost packet fatal?" — if yes, TCP; if retrying is worse than skipping, UDP.

blocks.subTitle: What is a port vs a socket?
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a port and a socket?**

A **port** is just a 16-bit number identifying a process on a host. A **socket** is the full endpoint: IP address + port. A connection is a pair of sockets. The port is part of the socket, not the same thing.

blocks.subTitle: Why UDP for video and games
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why is UDP used for video streaming and online games?**

TCP's retransmission blocks the stream — a lost packet forces a pause until it's resent, causing jitter. For live video, a dropped frame is invisible; a frozen frame ruins the call. UDP sends fresh data immediately; the app decides what to do with gaps.

**Q: What is multiplexing at the transport layer?**

Combining data from multiple processes into one outgoing packet stream (each stamped with a port), then at the receiver splitting it back — demultiplexing — to deliver each packet to the right process.
